summary: Covers arithmetic operators, integer division and truncation, modulus rules, pre-increment vs post-increment, relational and equality operators, logical operators and short-circuit evaluation, the conditional (ternary) operator, compound assignment operators, and full operator precedence hierarchies in C expressions.

key_terms.definition: Increments the operand variable before its value is evaluated in the enclosing expression.
Evaluates the current value of the operand variable first, then increments it after the expression evaluation.
A mechanism in logical operators (&& and ||) where evaluation ceases as soon as the outcome of the expression is determined.
C's three-operand conditional operator having syntax 'condition ? expr1 : expr2'.
Computes the remainder of integer division; invalid when applied to floating-point numbers.
Shorthand operators (+=, -=, *=, /=, %=) that combine an arithmetic operation with assignment.
The formal rules determining the order in which different operators are evaluated in an unparenthesized expression.
The direction (left-to-right or right-to-left) in which operators of the same precedence level are evaluated.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C code?
questions.explanation: '++x' is a pre-increment operator. It increments the value of 'x' from 2 to 3 first, and then supplies the updated value 3 to printf.

why_wrong.0: 2 would be the output if post-increment 'x++' were used.
why_wrong.2: Pre-increment adds 1 to x, it does not subtract.
why_wrong.3: Pre-increment inside printf is standard, valid C syntax.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q3; Deitel Ch 3.12

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C program?
questions.explanation: 'x++' is post-increment. The current value (2) is passed to the first printf before 'x' is incremented to 3. In the subsequent statement, 'x' evaluates to 3. Thus '2 3' is printed.

why_wrong.1: 3 3 would be printed if pre-increment '++x' had been used.
why_wrong.2: x is incremented after the first printf, so the second printf cannot print 2.
why_wrong.3: x is only incremented once.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C code?
questions.explanation: In C, when both operands of the division operator '/' are integers, integer division is performed. The fractional part is truncated (discarded), yielding 2. It does not produce a floating-point result or round up to 3.

why_wrong.1: 2.5 is the mathematical result, but integer division in C truncates all decimals.
why_wrong.2: C does not round 2.5 up to 3; it truncates toward zero.
why_wrong.3: Dividing two non-zero integers is completely valid C syntax.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q7; Deitel Ch 2.5

questions.question: Which of the following operators is used in C to compare two values for equality?
questions.explanation: '==' is the equality operator in C used to test if two expressions evaluate to the same value. '=' is the assignment operator, '+=' is addition assignment, and '&&' is logical AND.

why_wrong.0: '=' is the assignment operator that stores a value into a variable.
why_wrong.2: '+=' is a compound assignment operator that increments a variable by an amount.
why_wrong.3: '&&' is the logical AND operator that connects two boolean conditions.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q8; Deitel Ch 2.6

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C code?
questions.explanation: Multiplication '*' has higher operator precedence than addition '+'. Therefore, 'b * 2' is evaluated first (4 * 2 = 8), followed by addition 'a + 8' (3 + 8 = 11).

why_wrong.0: 14 is obtained if addition is evaluated first: (3 + 4) * 2 = 7 * 2 = 14.
why_wrong.2: 10 represents an arbitrary arithmetic error.
why_wrong.3: 7 would be (3 + 4).

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q15; Deitel Ch 2.5

questions.question: Which of the following correctly uses the conditional (ternary) operator in C?
options: a > b ? x = y : x = z;
if(a > b) x = y else x = z;
a > b : x = y ? x = z;
questions.explanation: The standard ternary syntax in C is 'variable = condition ? expr1 : expr2;'. Here, 'x = a > b ? y : z;' assigns y to x if a > b is true, or z to x if false.

why_wrong.0: In C, '=' has lower precedence than '?:', so 'a > b ? x = y : x = z' is syntactically invalid without parentheses.
why_wrong.1: This is an if-else statement without required semicolons, not the ternary operator.
why_wrong.2: The colon (:) and question mark (?) are reversed.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q18; Deitel Ch 3.5

questions.question: Which of the following is correct to increment an integer variable x by 1 in C?
questions.explanation: In standalone statements, all three constructs ('x = x + 1;', 'x++;', and '++x;') increment the value stored in variable x by exactly 1.

why_wrong.0: While correct, options B and C are also fully valid.
why_wrong.1: While correct, options A and C are also fully valid.
why_wrong.2: While correct, options A and B are also fully valid.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q20; Deitel Ch 3.12

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C code?
questions.explanation: The logical OR operator '||' evaluates to true (1) if either operand is non-zero. Since the right operand is 1 (non-zero/true), the condition (0 || 1) is true, and 'True' is printed.

why_wrong.1: False is only reached if both operands evaluate to 0.
why_wrong.2: The printf statement outputs the text 'True', not numeric 0.
why_wrong.3: The printf statement outputs the text 'True', not numeric 1.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q23; Deitel Ch 4.10

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C code?
questions.explanation: The condition 'x > y' (2 > 3) is false (0). The ternary operator selects the expression after the colon ':', which is 'y' (3). Thus 3 is printed.

why_wrong.0: 2 is 'x', which is only selected if x > y is true.
why_wrong.2: The ternary evaluates to the chosen operand's value, not boolean 0.
why_wrong.3: Using ternary expressions inside printf arguments is fully standard C.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q25; Deitel Ch 3.5

questions.question: Which of the following operators is used for the modulus (remainder) operation in C?
questions.explanation: The percent sign '%' is the modulus operator in C. It returns the remainder of integer division between its left and right operands.

why_wrong.2: '*' is the multiplication operator.
why_wrong.3: '+' is the addition operator.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q30; Deitel Ch 2.5

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C code?
questions.explanation: The logical AND operator '&&' requires both operands to be non-zero (true). Since 'y' is 0, the expression '1 && 0' evaluates to false, triggering the else clause to print 'No'.

why_wrong.0: Yes would require both x and y to be non-zero.
why_wrong.2: The code outputs the string 'No', not 1.
why_wrong.3: The code outputs the string 'No', not 0.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q33; Deitel Ch 4.10

questions.question: Which of the following is correct to increment a variable x by 2 in C?
questions.explanation: Both 'x += 2;' (compound addition assignment) and 'x = x + 2;' cleanly increment x by 2. Writing 'x++ + x++;' modifies x multiple times in an unsequenced expression, which causes Undefined Behavior in C.

why_wrong.0: 'x += 2;' is correct, but 'x = x + 2;' is also correct, making 'Both A and B' the comprehensive choice.
why_wrong.1: 'x = x + 2;' is correct, but 'x += 2;' is also correct.
why_wrong.2: 'x++ + x++;' invokes undefined behavior due to modifying the same scalar variable twice without an intervening sequence point.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q34; Deitel Ch 3.11

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C code?
questions.explanation: The condition 'x < y' (1 < 2) is true. In a ternary expression 'cond ? expr1 : expr2', when the condition is true, expr1 is selected. Here expr1 is 'y' (2). Therefore, 2 is printed.

why_wrong.0: 1 is 'x', which would be selected only if x < y were false.
why_wrong.2: The ternary yields the evaluated expression, not 0.
why_wrong.3: The syntax is valid standard C.

questions.source: COS 201 Midterm Type B, Q39; Deitel Ch 3.5

questions.question: What is the exact output of the following program demonstrating C's short-circuit behavior?
questions.explanation: In logical AND '&&', if the left operand evaluates to 0 (false), the entire expression is guaranteed false. C guarantees short-circuit evaluation: the right operand '++b' is NEVER executed. Consequently, 'b' remains 5, and 'a=0 b=5' is printed.

why_wrong.1: b=6 assumes '++b' was executed. Due to short-circuiting, it is completely skipped.
why_wrong.2: The if-branch is false, so 'Branch1' cannot print.
why_wrong.3: Expressions with side effects in if conditions are standard C.

questions.question: What will be printed by the following C program under the C99/C11 standard?
questions.explanation: Under standard C (C99 and later), the sign of the remainder resulting from the '%' operator matches the sign of the numerator (dividend): (-13) % 5 == -3, and 13 % (-5) == 3.

why_wrong.1: r2 has a positive numerator (13), so its remainder is positive (+3), not -3.
why_wrong.2: r1 has a negative numerator (-13), so its remainder is negative (-3).
why_wrong.3: 13 / 5 is 2 with remainder 3, not 2.

questions.question: What is the logical bug and resulting output in the following C code snippet?
options: Bug: '=' was used instead of '==', which assigns 1 to status and always prints 'Active'.
Bug: 'status = 1' produces a syntax error because assignment is forbidden in conditions.
Bug: 'Active' is printed because status was initially 0.
No bug: C interprets '=' as equality inside if conditions.
questions.explanation: Writing 'status = 1' inside the if condition is an assignment, not a comparison. It assigns 1 to 'status' and evaluates to the assigned value (1, which is true in C). As a result, the if condition always succeeds and prints 'Active'. The intended comparison was 'status == 1'.

why_wrong.1: Assignment inside if conditions is legal C syntax (though dangerous), generating a compiler warning, not an error.
why_wrong.2: Initial value 0 is overwritten by the assignment.
why_wrong.3: '=' is never interpreted as equality in C.

questions.question: What is the evaluated integer value of the C expression: 2 + 3 * 4 - 8 / 2 % 3?
questions.explanation:
Evaluating strictly by C operator precedence:
1. Multiplicative operators (*, /, %) from left-to-right:
   - 3 * 4 = 12
   - 8 / 2 = 4
   - 4 % 3 = 1
2. The expression simplifies to: 2 + 12 - 1
3. Additive operators (+, -) from left-to-right:
   - 2 + 12 = 14
   - 14 - 1 = 13.

pairs.right: Lower than logical OR; associates Right-to-Left

questions.explanation: Unary, ternary, and assignment operators associate Right-to-Left in C, whereas binary arithmetic and relational operators associate Left-to-Right.

questions.question: Order the sub-expression evaluations in C for: total = a + b * (c - d) / e;
steps: Multiply b by the parenthesized difference
Divide the multiplication result by e
Assign the final sum to total
questions.explanation: Parentheses (c - d) evaluate first. Multiplicative operators * and / then proceed left-to-right (multiply b, then divide by e). Addition (+ a) occurs next, and finally assignment (=) stores the result.

questions.question: Write a complete C main function that declares three integer variables: num1 = 45, num2 = 72, and max. Using a single ternary operator expression, assign the larger of num1 and num2 to max, and print 'Max: %d\n'.
marking_points: Uses ternary operator (num1 > num2) ? num1 : num2
Prints result using printf with format specifier %d
questions.explanation: Demonstrates concise conditional selection using the ternary operator without if-else statements.

questions.question: Explain the difference between pre-increment (++x) and post-increment (x++) in C. Provide a short code example illustrating when their evaluated values differ.
questions.answer:
1. In pre-increment (++x), the variable is incremented before its value is used in the enclosing expression.
2. In post-increment (x++), the current value of the variable is used in the enclosing expression first, and then the variable is incremented.
3. Example:
   int a = 5, b = 5;
   int x = ++a; // a becomes 6, x becomes 6
   int y = b++; // y becomes 5, b becomes 6
   Here, x and y receive different values even though both a and b end up as 6.
marking_points: Explains that pre-increment updates the variable before evaluation in the expression
Explains that post-increment evaluates the original value first, incrementing afterward
Provides a clear code example showing the value difference
questions.explanation: This distinction is one of the most frequently tested core C concepts across Nigerian universities.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C program?
questions.explanation: In mathematics, '10 < x < 20' checks if x is between 10 and 20. But in C, relational operators associate Left-to-Right! '10 < x' (10 < 25) evaluates to 1 (true). Then the expression becomes '1 < 20', which is also true (1)! Thus the if-condition succeeds and prints 'InRange', even though 25 is not less than 20. In C, range checking must be written as: (10 < x && x < 20).

why_wrong.1: OutRange would be correct mathematically, but C evaluates (10 < 25) -> 1, then (1 < 20) -> 1.
why_wrong.2: This is completely valid C syntax, though a notorious logic trap.
why_wrong.3: Behavior is fully defined by ISO C operator associativity.

questions.question: What is the output of the following C program comparing bitwise '&' and logical '&&'?
questions.explanation: Logical AND '&&' treats any non-zero value as true: (1 && 2) -> true (1). Bitwise AND '&' compares bits: 01 (binary 1) & 10 (binary 2) = 00 (binary 0). Output is '1 0'.

why_wrong.1: Bitwise 1 & 2 has no overlapping 1-bits, so it evaluates to 0, not 1.
why_wrong.2: Logical AND of two positive numbers is 1 (true), not 0.
why_wrong.3: Logical operators produce boolean results 0 or 1, not 2.

questions.question: What happens when the modulus operator '%' is used with floating-point operands in C (e.g. 5.5 % 2)?
options: Compilation error: operands must be of integral type.
It automatically truncates operands to integers before computing remainder.
It causes a runtime arithmetic crash.
questions.explanation: In C, the operands of the modulus operator '%' MUST have integer types (char, int, short, long). Applying '%' to float or double results in a compile-time error. (To compute remainder of floating-point numbers, the math library function 'fmod' from <math.h> must be used).

why_wrong.1: C does not support floating remainder via '%'; you must call fmod().
why_wrong.2: The compiler does not implicitly convert floats to integers for '%'; it rejects the code.
why_wrong.3: It is caught at compile-time, not at runtime.

questions.question: What does the modulus operator '%' do in C and what restriction does it have?
questions.answer: It returns the remainder of integer division. Restriction: Both operands MUST be integer types (illegal on float/double).

questions.question: What is the difference between '++x' and 'x++'?
questions.answer: '++x' increments first, then returns new value. 'x++' returns current value first, then increments.
questions.explanation: Pre-increment vs post-increment.

questions.question: What is short-circuit evaluation in C logical operators?
questions.answer: In '&&', if the first operand is 0 (false), the second is NOT evaluated. In '||', if the first operand is non-zero (true), the second is NOT evaluated.
questions.explanation: Guarantees no evaluation of right side when left side dictates outcome.

questions.question: What is the syntax and purpose of the conditional (ternary) operator?
questions.answer: Syntax: condition ? expr1 : expr2. If condition is true, evaluates to expr1; else evaluates to expr2.
questions.explanation: Only ternary operator in C.

questions.question: What is the danger of writing 'if (x = 0)' instead of 'if (x == 0)'?
questions.answer: 'x = 0' assigns 0 to x and evaluates to 0 (false), so the branch NEVER executes. '==' performs comparison.
questions.explanation: A classic C source bug.

questions.question: Between '*' and '+', which operator has higher precedence?
questions.answer: Multiplication '*' has higher precedence than addition '+'.
questions.explanation: Parentheses can be used to override default precedence.

questions.question: What is the associativity of assignment operators (=, +=, *=) in C?
questions.answer: Right-to-Left (e.g. a = b = c = 5 evaluates c=5 first, then b=5, then a=5).
questions.explanation: Unlike arithmetic operators which are Left-to-Right.

questions.question: What is 'x += 5' equivalent to in C?
questions.answer: 'x = x + 5' (adds 5 to the current value of x and stores result back in x).
questions.explanation: Compound assignment operator.

case_studies.title: Automated Nile Exam Grading Engine & Point Calculation
case_studies.scenario: A student in the Software Engineering department writes a grading snippet in C that converts raw scores into bonus points, computes remaining questions, and evaluates pass/fail status using ternary and compound assignment expressions. The code experiences unexpected results during test runs due to precedence and short-circuit misconceptions.

sub_questions.question: What is the output of the following score calculation snippet?
sub_questions.explanation: In compound assignment 'score += bonus * 2', the entire right-hand expression 'bonus * 2' is evaluated first (5 * 2 = 10). Then 'score += 10' executes: 50 + 10 = 60.

why_wrong.1: 110 would occur if (score + bonus) * 2 was evaluated: (50 + 5) * 2 = 110.
why_wrong.2: bonus is multiplied by 2, so it cannot be 55.
why_wrong.3: 100 is an arbitrary computation error.

sub_questions.question: What is printed by the nested ternary grade evaluation snippet?
sub_questions.explanation: The outer condition 'mark >= 70' (75 >= 70) is true. Therefore, the ternary operator directly evaluates to 'A' and does not evaluate the false branch '(mark >= 60) ? 'B' : 'F'.

why_wrong.1: Grade B is only evaluated if mark < 70.
why_wrong.2: Grade F is only evaluated if mark < 60.
why_wrong.3: Nested ternary expressions are completely valid standard C.

sub_questions.question: To award grace points, the system executes the following validation check. What will be printed?
sub_questions.explanation: In logical OR '||', the left operand is 'attendance > 80' (85 > 80), which evaluates to true (1). Because the first operand is true, C short-circuits: the right operand '++grace' is never evaluated. Thus 'grace' remains 0, printing 'Eligible: 0'.

why_wrong.1: Eligible: 1 is the trap if you assume ++grace was evaluated. Short-circuit skips ++grace.
why_wrong.2: The format string prints 'Eligible: %d' with the value.
why_wrong.3: The if-condition is true, so output is produced.

case_studies.title: Robotics Motor Speed Controller Logic
case_studies.scenario: A robotics control unit at Nile University monitors twin DC motor speeds and battery charge. Logic expressions regulate acceleration and safety cutoff limits.

sub_questions.question: A pulse generator pulses a motor every 3 clock cycles. What will this snippet output?
sub_questions.explanation: The modulus condition 't % 3 == 0' is true when t is an exact multiple of 3. In the range 1 to 6, this occurs at t=3 and t=6. Thus '3 6 ' is printed.

why_wrong.1: 1, 2, 4, 5 are the values where remainder is non-zero.
why_wrong.2: Loop starts at t = 1, so t = 0 is never evaluated.
why_wrong.3: t = 6 also satisfies 6 % 3 == 0.

sub_questions.question: What is the output of the following speed synchronization step?
sub_questions.explanation: '++speed' increments speed from 10 to 11 first. Then 11 + 5 = 16 is assigned to target. Both variables reflect this: speed=11, target=16.

why_wrong.1: speed was incremented, so it cannot remain 10.
why_wrong.2: target is 11 + 5 = 16, not 15.
why_wrong.3: speed was incremented to 11.
